## [4]{.num} Methodological pluralism {.divider}

::: {.lines}
Whether one method fits all research
:::

::: {.notes}
**Time.** This section runs 3.5 minutes. The toolkit slide takes 1, Leonelli 1.5 and reproducibility 1.

**Where this fits.** The textbook picture from section 2 is the confirmatory experiment. This section tests whether that one method describes all research.
:::

## What the toolkit asks of research {.s4}

- A hypothesis fixed before the data
- A study someone else could repeat
- Data apart from the people who made them

::: {.prompt .fragment}
Open science assumes one method fits all research
:::

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1 minute.

**Run it.** Read the three features. Press the arrow key once and say the assumption aloud.

**The toolkit.** Preregistration and registered reports ask a researcher to fix a hypothesis before collecting data. Replication asks that someone else repeat a study. Data sharing treats data as separable from the people who made them.

**Point.** Each tool fits some kinds of research and not others. Open science often presents them as the way to do science. Leonelli and the reproducibility slide follow.
:::

## One policy, many kinds of research {.s4}

::: {.lines}
Standardized, top-down open science policy can entrench some kinds of research

::: {.fragment}
and the inequities that come with them
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1.5 minutes.

**Leonelli 2022.**

- Sabina Leonelli published "Open Science and Epistemic Diversity: Friends or Foes?" in *Philosophy of Science* 89(5), December 2022, pp. 991–1001.
- She argues that standardized, top-down open science policy ignores epistemic diversity and risks entrenching some forms of research and some inequities.
- Her book *Philosophy of Open Science* (Cambridge Elements, 2023) goes further. It argues that treating openness as resource sharing narrows epistemic diversity and worsens epistemic injustice, and it proposes openness as well-considered connections between systems of practice.

**Implementation.** Policy decides how open science is implemented, and a mandate designed around one kind of research can flatten the others.
:::

## What reproducibility means {.s4}

::: {.boxes .tight .small}
::: {.box}
[Methods]{.boxlabel}

Repeat the procedures as exactly as possible.
:::
::: {.box .fragment}
[Results]{.boxlabel}

A new study corroborates the results.
:::
::: {.box .fragment}
[Inferential]{.boxlabel}

A replication or reanalysis supports claims of similar strength.
:::
:::

::: {.prompt .fragment}
Open data serves some kinds of reproducibility and not others
:::

::: {.notes}
**Time.** 1 minute.

**Run it.** Press the arrow key once for each of the other two boxes, and once more for the closing line.

**The three kinds.** Goodman, Fanelli and Ioannidis separate reproducibility into three kinds in "What does research reproducibility mean?" (*Science Translational Medicine* 8(341): 341ps12, June 1, 2016).

- **Methods reproducibility** means implementing the procedures as exactly as possible. It needs the data, the code and a full account of the procedures.
- **Results reproducibility** means corroborating the results in a new study. It needs a new study, and the original data play little part.
- **Inferential reproducibility** means a replication or reanalysis supports knowledge claims of similar strength. It depends on judgment about what counts as similar.

The three definitions come from secondary sources, because the journal page was unreachable when the deck was built. Read the paper before you quote them.

**Link to the room.** Ask which kind of reproducibility fits the research the students know best, and which kinds it does not allow.

**Point.** Open data serves methods reproducibility most directly. Results and inferential reproducibility ask for new studies and judgment, so which kind matters depends on the research.
:::
